documents.t: This guide explains how to parse and serialize HL7 messages using the WSO2 Open Healthcare. The WSO2 Open Healthcare provides a set of built-in capabilities to parse and serialize HL7 messages using a user-friendly graphical tooling. The tooling allows you to parse HL7 messages and extract message fields using visual data mapping features.

The following example demonstrates how to parse an HL7v2 ADT_A01 message using Ballerina. The example defines a custom patient record and a data mapping function to extract the patient record from an ADT_A01 message.

Open WSO2 Integrator. Select Create in the Create New Integration card. Set Integration Name to HL7MessageParse. Set Project Name to hl7-message-parse. Select Create Integration. Select Add Artifact and select Automation.

Import the required modules and implement the Ballerina program. In this sample, we are using ADT_A01 message from HL7v2.3 version. Therefore, we need to import ballerinax/health.hl7v23 package. If you are using a different version of HL7, you can import the relevant package. You need to use parse function from ballerinax/health.hl7v2 package to parse the HL7 message. import ballerina/io; import ballerinax/health.hl7v2 as hl7; import ballerinax/health.hl7v23 as hl7v23; // The following example is a simple serialized HL v2.3 ADT A01 message. final string msg = "MSH|^~\\&|ADT1|GOOD HEALTH HOSPITAL|GHH LAB, INC.|GOOD HEALTH HOSPITAL|" + "198808181126|SECURITY|ADT^A01^ADT_A01|MSG00001|P|2.3||\rEVN|A01|200708181123||" + "\rPID|1||PATID1234^5^M11^ADT1^MR^GOOD HEALTH HOSPITAL~123456789^^^USSSA^SS||" + "BATMAN^ADAM^A^III||19610615|M||C|2222 HOME STREET^^GREENSBORO^NC^27401-1020|GL|" + "(555) 555-2004|(555)555-2004||S||PATID12345001^2^M10^ADT1^AN^A|444333333|987654^NC|" + "\rNK1|1|NUCLEAR^NELDA^W|SPO^SPOUSE||||NK^NEXT OF KIN$\rPV1|1|I|2000^2012^01||||" + "004777^ATTEND^AARON^A|||SUR||||ADM|A0|"; public function main() returns error? { // This message, ADT^A01 is an HL7 data type consisting of several components, so we // will cast it as such. The ADT_A01 class extends from Message, providing specialized // accessors for ADT^A01's segments. // // Ballerina HL7 provides several versions of the ADT_A01 record type, each in a // different package (note the import statement above) corresponding to the HL7 // version for the message. hl7v23:ADT_A01 adtMsg = check hl7:parse(msg).ensureType(hl7v23:ADT_A01); // Access the fields of the ADT_A01 message. hl7v23:XPN[] patientName = adtMsg.pid.pid5; io:println("Family Name: ", patientName[0].xpn1); }

The following example demonstrates how to serialize (encode) an HL7v2 QRY_A19 message using Ballerina.

Open WSO2 Integrator. Select Create in the Create New Integration card. Set Integration Name to HL7MessageSerialize. Set Project Name to hl7-message-serialize. Select Create Integration. Select Add Artifact and select Automation.

Import the required modules and implement the Ballerina program. In this sample we will be populating a QRY_A19 message from HL7v2.3 and serializing it to the wire format. import ballerinax/health.hl7v2; import ballerinax/health.hl7v23; import ballerina/io; public function main() returns error? { hl7v23:QRY_A19 qry_a19 = { msh: { msh3: {hd1: "ADT1"}, msh4: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh5: {hd1: "LABADT"}, msh6: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh8: "SECURITY", msh9: {cm_msg1: "QRY", cm_msg2: "A19"}, msh10: "MSG00001", msh11: {pt1: "P"}, msh12: "2.3" }, qrd: { qrd1: {ts1: "20220828104856+0000"}, qrd2: "R", qrd3: "I", qrd4: "QueryID01", qrd7: {cq1: "5"}, qrd8: [{xcn1: "1", xcn2: "ADAM", xcn3: "EVERMAN"}], qrd9: [{ce1: "VXI"}], qrd10: [{ce1: "SIIS"}] } }; // Serialize the QRY_A19 message to a byte array using the encode function. You can use the encoded message to // send over the wire to a HL7 server. byte[] encodedQRYA19 = check hl7v2:encode(hl7v23:VERSION, qry_a19); // Print the encoded string io:println(string `Encoded string: ${check string:fromBytes(encodedQRYA19)}`); }

This guide explains how to populate HL7 messages using the WSO2 Open Healthcare. The WSO2 Open Healthcare provides a set of built-in capabilities to construct HL7 messages using a user-friendly graphical tooling. The tooling allows you to create HL7 messages by selecting the message type or feeding the message schema and populating the message fields using visual data mapping features. The following example demonstrates how to populate an HL7v2 ADT_A01 message using Ballerina. The example defines a custom patient record and a data mapping function to convert the patient record to an ADT_A01 message.

Open WSO2 Integrator. Select Create in the Create New Integration card. Set Integration Name to HL7MessagePopulate. Set Project Name to hl7-message-populate. Select Create Integration. Select Add Artifact and select Automation.

Import the required modules to the Ballerina program. In this sample we are using ADT_A01 message from HL7v2.3 version. Therefore, we need to import ballerinax/health.hl7v23 package. If you are using a different version of HL7, you can import the relevant package. import ballerinax/health.hl7v2; import ballerinax/health.hl7v23; import ballerina/io; Create a custom patient record type to represent the patient data. In this sample, the patient record contains the patient's first name, last name, address, and phone number. // A custom patient record. type Patient record { string firstName; string lastName; string address; string phoneNumber; }; Define a data mapping function to convert the patient record to an ADT_A01 message. The function takes the patient record as input and returns an ADT_A01 message. You can use the visual data mapper in ballerina to map the patient record fields to the ADT_A01 message fields. You can follow the documentation on Visual Data Mapping to learn more about visual data mapping in Ballerina. // Data mapping function to convert a patient record to an ADT_A01 message. function patientToAdtA01(Patient patient) returns hl7v23:ADT_A01 => { msh: { msh3: {hd1: "ADT1"}, msh4: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh5: {hd1: "LABADT"}, msh6: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh8: "SECURITY", msh9: {cm_msg1: "ADT", cm_msg2: "A01"}, msh10: "MSG00001", msh11: {pt1: "P"}, msh12: "2.3" }, pid: { pid5: [{xpn1: patient.lastName, xpn2: patient.firstName}], pid11: [{xad1: patient.address}], pid13: [{xtn1: patient.phoneNumber}] }, pv1: {}, evn: {} }; Serialize the ADT_A01 message to a string using the hl7:encode function. The complete code sample will look as follows: import ballerinax/health.hl7v2; import ballerinax/health.hl7v23; import ballerina/io; // A custom patient record. type Patient record { string firstName; string lastName; string address; string phoneNumber; }; public function main() returns error? { // Sample patient data Patient patient = {firstName: "John", lastName: "Doe", address: "123 Main St", phoneNumber: "555-555-5555"}; hl7v23:ADT_A01 adtMsg2 = patientToAdtA01(patient); // Serialize the ADT_A01 message to a string. string adtMsgStr = check string:fromBytes(check hl7:encode("2.3", adtMsg2)); io:println(adtMsgStr); } // Data mapping function to convert a patient record to an ADT_A01 message. function patientToAdtA01(Patient patient) returns hl7v23:ADT_A01 => { msh: { msh3: {hd1: "ADT1"}, msh4: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh5: {hd1: "LABADT"}, msh6: {hd1: "MCM"}, msh8: "SECURITY", msh9: {cm_msg1: "ADT", cm_msg2: "A01"}, msh10: "MSG00001", msh11: {pt1: "P"}, msh12: "2.3" }, pid: { pid5: [{xpn1: patient.lastName, xpn2: patient.firstName}], pid11: [{xad1: patient.address}], pid13: [{xtn1: patient.phoneNumber}] }, pv1: {}, evn: {} };

This guide walks through the steps to generate an OpenAPI specification from a FHIR Implementation Guide using the Ballerina Health Tool, and then deploy it as a managed API in WSO2 API Manager using the FHIR Repository as the backend.

Install and setup WSO2 Open Healthcare. Install the Ballerina CLI, Swan Lake 2201.12.0 (Update 12) or later. The Health Tool commands below run with bal. A FHIR Implementation Guide (IG) to generate the API.

The Ballerina Health Tool can generate an OpenAPI specification and a Ballerina project template directly from a FHIR Implementation Guide. Pull the Ballerina Health Tool: bal tool pull health Run the FHIR template generation command, pointing to your Implementation Guide package: bal health gen fhir -m template --org-name [ORG_NAME] [IG_PACKAGE_NAME] Replace the placeholders with: [ORG_NAME]: Your Ballerina organization name (e.g., healthcare) [IG_PACKAGE_NAME]: The Ballerina package name of the FHIR IG (e.g., ballerinax/health.fhir.r4.uscore501) Example: bal health gen fhir -m template --org-name healthcare ballerinax/health.fhir.r4.uscore501 The tool generates a Ballerina project with: An OpenAPI specification (OAS) file for each FHIR resource in the IG. A Ballerina service template with boilerplate FHIR resource handlers. Locate the generated OAS file(s) in the output directory. These will be used to create the API in WSO2 API Manager. tip For standard FHIR R4 APIs without a custom IG, you can skip this step and directly download a pre-built OAS file from the FHIR API Definitions page.
documents.s: Step 1 - Generate OpenAPI Specification from a FHIR Implementation Guide

documents.t: Log in to the WSO2 APIM Publisher Portal at https://localhost:9443/publisher. Click Create API and select Import Open API. Upload the OAS file generated in Step 1 and click Next. Fill in the API details: Name: e.g., USCorePatientAPI Context: e.g., /fhir/r4 Version: e.g., 1.0.0 Endpoint URL: The URL of the running Ballerina FHIR service (e.g., http://localhost:9090/r4) Click Create to create the API. In the API overview, go to Deployments and click Deploy: Select the target Gateway (e.g., Default). Click Deploy. Go to Lifecycle and click Publish to make the API available in the Developer Portal. note Ensure the WSO2 APIM gateway can reach the Ballerina FHIR service endpoint. If running locally, use host.docker.internal instead of localhost when APIM runs in Docker.
documents.s: Step 2 - Create and Deploy the API in WSO2 API Manager

documents.t: Navigate to the Developer Portal at https://localhost:9443/devportal. Find the published FHIR API and confirm it appears in the portal. Invoke the well-known endpoint to verify the FHIR gateway is responding: curl https://localhost:8243/r4/.well-known/smart-configuration Test a FHIR resource endpoint: curl https://localhost:8243/r4/metadata A valid FHIR CapabilityStatement response confirms the API is deployed and the FHIR backend is reachable.

WSO2 Updates include improvements that are released by WSO2, on top of a released WSO2 product version. With updates, you do not have to wait until the next product version release to get the product enhancements and security fixes. Read more about WSO2 latest update tool.
A subscription is required to receive WSO2 updates. Subscriptions are available in different tiers to suit your requirements. Read more about WSO2 subscription model

It is imperative to update your products frequently. It will ensure your environment has the latest improvements and the bug fixes. In case you are faced with an issue in your environment, if this has been fixed in an update already and you have missed a recent update, it is possible that the issue is already fixed in a more recent update. Whenever WSO2 releases a security update, we inform our customers at our earliest. WSO2 always recommends applying security updates sooner whenever we release a security update. This will ensure your production environment is secure.

Update Tool client delivers hotfixes and updates seamlessly on top of the product pack. The Update Tool is available in each product release distribution and is located at <product-home>/bin directory.

documents.t: Download the IS accelerator for WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0, wso2-hcis-accelerator-2.1.0.zip, and extract it. Copy the extracted accelerator folder to <WSO2_IS_HOME>. This guide calls it <WSO2_OH_IS_ACC_HOME>. Optional: enable or disable features in <WSO2_OH_IS_ACC_HOME>/conf/config.toml. See Accelerator configuration options. Run the merge script from <WSO2_OH_IS_ACC_HOME>/bin: ./merge.sh tip merge.sh backs up the product files it replaces, so you can tell what changed or restore them. See the details below. What merge.sh changes The first run creates an hc-accelerator folder in the product home, with a backup folder and a merge_audit.log file. backup holds the original product files from before the first run. Later runs keep this backup and don't overwrite it, so it always reflects the unmodified product. It contains: API Manager: conf/deployment.toml, conf/claim-config.xml, and the accountrecoveryendpoint and authenticationendpoint web apps under webapps. Identity Server: conf/deployment.toml. If the consent portal's config.js exists from an earlier deployment, it's also saved and restored after the merge. merge_audit.log gets one line per run, with the date and time, the user, and the accelerator version. For example: Mon May 31 22:01:55 +0530 2021 - john - WSO2 Open Healthcare API Manager 1.0.0 Accelerator - v1.0.0

This section provides step-by-step instructions to configure WSO2 Identity Server 7.x as a Key Manager for WSO2 API Manager, enabling secure API access and management. Sign in to the Admin Portal of API Manager at https://localhost:9443/admin. Go to Key Managers on the left main menu. Configure WSO2 IS 7.x as a keymanager. This quick start walks you through building a FHIR R4 Patient API facade with WSO2 Integrator. The facade sits in front of a WSO2 FHIR Server repository, proxies Patient read and search requests to it, and changes each response before it reaches the client. You describe the facade to WSO2 Integrator Copilot in plain language, then review the generated flows in the low-code view.

A hospital stores Patient records in a FHIR repository. Client apps need access to those records, but must not see Social Security numbers or full phone numbers. Instead of changing the repository, you put a facade in front of it that: Removes identifiers with the system http://hl7.org/fhir/sid/us-ssn. Masks phone numbers so that only the last 4 digits are visible, for example ***-***-4412. Tags every Patient with a patient-api-facade meta.tag, so clients can tell the data came through the facade. Hides the repository address by rewriting the Bundle link and fullUrl values to the facade's own base URL. You will: Start the WSO2 FHIR Server and load sample Patients. Create an integration project in WSO2 Integrator. Generate the facade with WSO2 Integrator Copilot. Review the read, search, and response-change flows in the low-code view. Run the facade and compare its responses with the repository's.

You enter this prompt in Step 4: Create a FHIR R4 Patient API facade in front of a WSO2 FHIR Server repository. Expose an HTTP service on port 9091 with the base path /fhir/r4. Read the repository base URL from a configurable named fhirServerUrl with the default value http://localhost:9090/fhir/r4, and read the facade's own base URL from a configurable named facadeBaseUrl with the default value http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4. Call the repository with the ballerinax/health.clients.fhir FHIRConnector. Use the ballerinax/health.fhir.r4 and ballerinax/health.fhir.r4.international401 packages for the FHIR types, and return responses with the application/fhir+json content type. 1. GET /Patient/{id}: read the Patient from the repository. If it does not exist, return HTTP 404 with a FHIR OperationOutcome. 2. GET /Patient: forward all query parameters (for example family, gender and _count) to the repository search and return the searchset Bundle. Apply these facade changes to every Patient the facade returns, both from a read and from each entry of a search Bundle. For search results, convert each Bundle entry resource to an international401:Patient (for example with toJson() and cloneWithType()), apply the changes, and put the changed Patient back into the entry: - Remove identifiers with the system http://hl7.org/fhir/sid/us-ssn. - Mask every phone number in telecom so that only the last 4 digits are visible, for example ***-***-4412. - Add a meta.tag with system http://wso2.com/fhir/facade/source and code patient-api-facade. In search Bundles, also replace the repository base URL with facadeBaseUrl in every link url and entry fullUrl, so clients never see the repository address. If the repository is unreachable or returns an error, return HTTP 502 with an OperationOutcome. note Copilot output is AI-generated and can differ between runs. The flows and code in this guide are from one run of this prompt. Always review the generated changes, and test the facade before you rely on it.

WSO2 Integrator installed. It includes the Ballerina distribution, so you don't need to install Ballerina separately. Signed in to WSO2 Integrator Copilot with your WSO2 account. Docker with Docker Compose (or an alternative such as Rancher Desktop or Colima) to run the WSO2 FHIR Server. curl or any HTTP client for testing.

Download the WSO2 FHIR Server Docker Compose file and start the stack. It runs the FHIR Server on port 9090 with a PostgreSQL database, and creates the database tables on first start: curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/fhir-server/main/docker-compose.yml docker compose up -d Check that the server is ready: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:9090/health/ready # Expect: 200 The FHIR base URL is http://localhost:9090/fhir/r4. note The stack also uses port 5432 for PostgreSQL and port 8080 for the Adminer database UI. Stop anything else using ports 9090, 5432, or 8080 before you start it. If the image pull fails with denied, Docker may have expired credentials saved for ghcr.io. The image is public, so run docker logout ghcr.io and try again.

documents.t: Save this transaction Bundle as patients-bundle.json. documents.t: Close the Copilot panel to see the service design. The HTTP listener feeds the /fhir/r4 service, and both resources call the repository through the fhirServerClient connection. Click a resource or function to open its flow. Each node maps to a statement in the source code. Use the Low-code view and Source code tabs below to compare them.
documents.s: Step 5: Review the flows in the low-code view

documents.t: The GET /Patient/[string id] flow: Calls getById on the fhirServerClient connection. Returns HTTP 404 when the repository reports the Patient as not found, and HTTP 502 for any other repository error or when the repository is unreachable. Converts the payload to an international401:Patient, applies the facade changes, and returns it. Low-code view Source code Repository call and error handling: Response changes and return: resource function get Patient/[string id]() returns http:Response { fhir:FHIRResponse|fhir:FHIRServerError|fhir:FHIRConnectorError result = fhirServerClient->getById("Patient", id); if result is fhir:FHIRServerError { int statusCode = result.detail().httpStatusCode; if statusCode == 404 { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildNotFoundOutcome(string `Patient/${id} not found`), 404); } return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome(string `Repository returned an error for Patient/${id}`), 502); } if result is fhir:FHIRConnectorError { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome(string `Repository is unreachable for Patient/${id}`), 502); } json|xml resourcePayload = result.'resource; international401:Patient|error patient = trap resourcePayload.cloneWithType(international401:Patient); if patient is error { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome(string `Repository returned an invalid Patient payload for Patient/${id}`), 502); } international401:Patient changedPatient = applyFacadeChanges(patient); return buildJsonResponse(changedPatient.toJson(), 200); }

The applyFacadeChanges function holds the response changes. It filters out SSN identifiers, masks each phone number with maskIfPhone, and adds the facade tag to meta.tag, keeping any tags the repository already set. Low-code view Source code isolated function applyFacadeChanges(international401:Patient patient) returns international401:Patient { r4:Identifier[]? identifiers = patient.identifier; if identifiers is r4:Identifier[] { patient.identifier = from r4:Identifier identifier in identifiers where identifier.system != US_SSN_IDENTIFIER_SYSTEM select identifier; } r4:ContactPoint[]? telecom = patient.telecom; if telecom is r4:ContactPoint[] { patient.telecom = from r4:ContactPoint contactPoint in telecom select maskIfPhone(contactPoint); } r4:Meta? meta = patient.meta; r4:Coding facadeTag = {system: FACADE_TAG_SYSTEM, code: FACADE_TAG_CODE}; if meta is r4:Meta { r4:Coding[]? tags = meta.tag; if tags is r4:Coding[] { tags.push(facadeTag); meta.tag = tags; } else { meta.tag = [facadeTag]; } patient.meta = meta; } else { patient.meta = {tag: [facadeTag]}; } return patient; } isolated function maskIfPhone(r4:ContactPoint contactPoint) returns r4:ContactPoint { r4:ContactPointSystem? system = contactPoint.system; string? value = contactPoint.value; if system == r4:phone && value is string { contactPoint.value = maskPhoneNumber(value); } return contactPoint; }

The GET /Patient flow: Forwards every query parameter, including _count, to the repository's search. Returns HTTP 502 when the repository fails or returns an invalid Bundle. Loops over the Bundle entries and applies the facade changes to each Patient with applyFacadeChangesToEntry. Rewrites the Bundle link and entry fullUrl values to facadeBaseUrl with rewriteBundleUrls. Low-code view Source code resource function get Patient(http:Request request) returns http:Response { map<string[]> searchParameters = request.getQueryParams(); fhir:FHIRResponse|fhir:FHIRServerError|fhir:FHIRConnectorError result = fhirServerClient->search("Patient", searchParameters); if result is fhir:FHIRServerError { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome("Repository returned an error for Patient search"), 502); } if result is fhir:FHIRConnectorError { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome("Repository is unreachable for Patient search"), 502); } json|xml resourcePayload = result.'resource; r4:Bundle|error bundle = trap resourcePayload.cloneWithType(r4:Bundle); if bundle is error { return buildOutcomeResponse(buildBadGatewayOutcome("Repository returned an invalid Bundle payload for Patient search"), 502); } r4:BundleEntry[]? entries = bundle.entry; if entries is r4:BundleEntry[] { r4:BundleEntry[] changedEntries = []; foreach r4:BundleEntry entry in entries { r4:BundleEntry|error changedEntry = applyFacadeChangesToEntry(entry); if changedEntry is error { changedEntries.push(entry); continue; } changedEntries.push(changedEntry); } bundle.entry = changedEntries; } r4:Bundle rewrittenBundle = rewriteBundleUrls(bundle); return buildJsonResponse(rewrittenBundle.toJson(), 200); } isolated function applyFacadeChangesToEntry(r4:BundleEntry entry) returns r4:BundleEntry|error { anydata|r4:FHIRWireFormat resource = entry.'resource; if resource is () { return entry; } json resourceJson = check resource.cloneWithType(json); international401:Patient patient = check resourceJson.cloneWithType(international401:Patient); international401:Patient changedPatient = applyFacadeChanges(patient); entry.'resource = changedPatient.toJson(); return entry; } caution If an entry can't be converted to a Patient, this generated code passes it through unchanged, without the facade changes. For a production facade that must never leak sensitive data, change the changedEntry is error branch to drop the entry or fail the request instead.

Click Run in the integration's toolbar. WSO2 Integrator compiles the integration and starts it in the Terminal panel. The facade is ready when the terminal shows Running executable. The facade listens at http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4/Patient and proxies to the repository at http://localhost:9090/fhir/r4. To point it at a different repository, set fhirServerUrl in Config.toml or with Configure.

Read Alice Smith from the repository directly. Replace {id} with her id from Step 2: curl -s "http://localhost:9090/fhir/r4/Patient/{id}" The repository returns the full record, including the SSN and the full phone number: { "resourceType": "Patient", "id": "04c9555f-5dce-4bef-be99-c24201b48d41", "meta": {"versionId": "1", "lastUpdated": "2026-10-30T14:05:55+05:30"}, "identifier": [ {"system": "http://hospital.example.org/mrn", "value": "MRN-100234"}, {"system": "http://hl7.org/fhir/sid/us-ssn", "value": "123-45-6789"} ], "name": [{"family": "Smith", "given": ["Alice"]}], "telecom": [ {"system": "phone", "use": "mobile", "value": "555-201-4412"}, {"system": "email", "value": "alice.smith@example.org"} ], "gender": "female", "birthDate": "1990-05-15" } Now read the same Patient through the facade: curl -s "http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4/Patient/{id}" The facade returns HTTP 200 with application/fhir+json. The SSN is gone, the phone number is masked, the email is unchanged, and the facade tag is added: { "resourceType": "Patient", "id": "04c9555f-5dce-4bef-be99-c24201b48d41", "meta": { "versionId": "1", "lastUpdated": "2026-10-30T14:05:55+05:30", "tag": [{"system": "http://wso2.com/fhir/facade/source", "code": "patient-api-facade"}] }, "identifier": [{"system": "http://hospital.example.org/mrn", "value": "MRN-100234"}], "name": [{"family": "Smith", "given": ["Alice"]}], "telecom": [ {"system": "phone", "value": "***-***-4412", "use": "mobile"}, {"system": "email", "value": "alice.smith@example.org"} ], "gender": "female", "birthDate": "1990-05-15" }

curl -s "http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4/Patient?family=Smith" Expected: a searchset Bundle with Alice and Robert Smith. Each entry has the facade changes applied: no SSN, masked phone numbers (***-***-4412 and ***-***-7788), and the patient-api-facade tag. The link and fullUrl values point to http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4, not the repository. Query parameters are passed through to the repository. Add _count=1 to get one entry per page, with a next link that also uses the facade's URL: curl -s "http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4/Patient?family=Smith&_count=1"
curl -s "http://localhost:9091/fhir/r4/Patient/does-not-exist" Expected: HTTP 404 with an OperationOutcome with code not-found.
documents.s: Read a Patient that doesn't exist

documents.t: Stop the WSO2 FHIR Server, then repeat the read or search through the facade: docker compose stop server Expected: HTTP 502 with an OperationOutcome with severity fatal, for example Repository is unreachable for Patient search. Start the server again with docker compose start server to restore normal responses. The data is stored in PostgreSQL, so the sample Patients are still there.

Healthcare APIs play a pivotal role in modern healthcare by enabling systems to seamlessly exchange data across platforms, such as Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) and mobile health applications. However, the sensitive nature of healthcare data, including personal health information (PHI), makes API security a top priority. Unsecured APIs can expose healthcare systems to data breaches, privacy violations, and compliance risks. Therefore, adopting secure practices is essential to maintain the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of patient data.
documents.s: Securing Health APIs: Why it is essential?

documents.t: SMART on FHIR (Substitutable Medical Applications, Reusable Technologies) is an open standard for enabling third-party healthcare applications to securely access FHIR resources. SMART on FHIR provides a framework for building secure and interoperable APIs in healthcare. It combines the FHIR standard for data exchange with OAuth 2.0 for authentication and authorization, ensuring secure access to healthcare data. The following are the key ways SMART on FHIR strengthens API security: OAuth 2.0 for Authentication and Authorization Authorization Code Grant Flow requires users to authenticate with their identity provider (e.g., hospital system or EMR) before receiving an access token. This flow guarantees that apps cannot access health data unless authorized by the user (e.g., clinician or patient). OAuth also supports refresh tokens to extend access securely without re-authentication. Role-based access control with scopes SMART on FHIR APIs use OAuth scopes to limit what an app can access. Most commonly used scopes are as below. openid fhirUser: Permission to retrieve information about the current logged-in user. launch/patient: When launching outside the EHR, ask for a patient to be selected at launch time. offline_access: Request a refresh token that can be used to obtain a new access token to replace an expired one, even after the end-user no longer is online after the access token expires. Identity Management and OpenID Connect (OIDC) SMART on FHIR integrates with OpenID Connect to provide identity verification for users. This ensures that healthcare apps can securely verify the identity of the patient or clinician requesting access. Token-Based Access for Enhanced Security After authentication, SMART on FHIR uses short-lived tokens (OAuth access tokens) to access APIs. Tokens expire quickly, reducing the window of opportunity for unauthorized use if stolen. Applications can request refresh tokens to renew access without asking the user to log in again, maintaining a balance between security and convenience.
documents.s: How SMART on FHIR builds secure APIs

documents.t: The following diagram shows the key components involved in a SMART on FHIR deployment using WSO2 Open Healthcare and how they interact during the authorization and API access flow.

Below are the key steps involved in launching a SMART app and gaining access to FHIR APIs for seamless data exchange. Launch App: Standalone Launch or EHR Launch A SMART app can be launched in two ways: Standalone Launch: The app initiates the login process independently. For example, a patient-facing health web app where the user logs in through an external identity provider connected to the EHR system. EHR Launch: The app is opened within the context of an EHR session. For example, a clinician-facing app used during a patient visit, where the EHR passes a launch token containing relevant patient or encounter information to the app. Retrieve .well-known/smart-configuration The app retrieves the EHR’s .well-known/smart-configuration file to obtain OAuth 2.0 endpoints (authorization and token endpoints) and discover supported scopes and other relevant data for authorization. This step ensures the app interacts with the correct endpoints for secure access. Obtain Authorization Code The app redirects the user to the authorization endpoint. The user authenticates using their credentials and grants consent to allow the app access to specific scopes. The EHR issues an authorization code to the app through the redirect URI. This code serves as a temporary credential to request an access token. Obtain Access Token The app exchanges the authorization code for an access token by calling the EHR’s token endpoint. The request includes the client ID, client secret, authorization code, and redirect URI. If successful, the EHR returns an access token. The access token grants the app permission to interact with FHIR APIs on behalf of the user. Access FHIR API With the access token in hand, the app makes API requests to the EHR’s FHIR server. For example: GET /Patient/{id} to retrieve a patient’s demographics. GET /Observation?patient={id} to access lab results. Each API request includes the access token in the HTTP header (Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>). SMART on FHIR Compliance WSO2 Open Healthcare is compliant with the SMART App Launch STU2.2 specification. You can download the full test report below. Download SMART App Launch STU2 Test Report
SMART App Launch — HL7 specification OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749) OpenID Connect specification

Comprehensive audit logging is essential for healthcare compliance (HIPAA, GDPR) and security monitoring. WSO2 Open Healthcare records FHIR interactions as AuditEvent resources through a dedicated audit service that integrates with FHIR facade APIs built using the Ballerina FHIR R4 service type.

When audit logging is enabled on a FHIR API, each completed request produces an audit record that captures: Who accessed or modified data (agent identification) What resources were accessed (entity tracking) When the action occurred (timestamp) Where the request originated (source observer) How the access was performed (REST interaction and action code) Outcome of the request (success or failure)

The WSO2 Healthcare Accelerator includes a pre-built Audit Service that accepts flattened audit payloads and persists them as FHIR R4 AuditEvent resources. The service is available in the open-healthcare-choreo-accelerators repository under miscellaneous/audit-service.

Accepts audit events via a lightweight REST API (POST /audits) Converts incoming payloads to FHIR R4 AuditEvent resources with terminology-backed codings Appends audit events as newline-delimited JSON to a configurable log file Buffers failed writes in an in-memory cache and retries on a scheduled interval
Operation Endpoint Description Post audit event POST /audits Accept an audit payload and persist it as an AuditEvent The service listens on port 9093 by default.

The audit service accepts an InternalAuditEvent payload—a flattened representation of key AuditEvent fields: Field Maps to Description typeCode AuditEvent.type Event type (default: rest) subTypeCode AuditEvent.subtype REST interaction (for example, read, create, search-type) actionCode AuditEvent.action Action performed (R, C, U, D, or E) outcomeCode AuditEvent.outcome 0 for success, 8 for failure recordedTime AuditEvent.recorded UTC timestamp of the event agentType AuditEvent.agent.type Security role of the agent agentName AuditEvent.agent.who.display Display name or ID of the agent agentIsRequestor AuditEvent.agent.requestor Whether the agent initiated the request sourceObserverName AuditEvent.source.observer.display Name of the observing system sourceObserverType AuditEvent.source.type Source type code entityType AuditEvent.entity.type Type of entity accessed entityRole AuditEvent.entity.role Role of the entity in the event entityWhatReference AuditEvent.entity.what.reference Relative path of the resource (for example, Patient/example)

Configure the audit service in Config.toml: # Path to the audit log file (use a mounted volume in production) auditLogPath = "/tmp/audit-logs/fhir-audit.log" # Capacity of the in-memory cache for failed writes cacheCapacity = 1000 # Default FHIR server name used as the source observer when not provided fhirServerName = "wso2fhirserver.com" # Default agent type when not provided in the payload agentType = "humanuser"

Clone the accelerator repository and start the audit service: git clone https://github.com/wso2/open-healthcare-choreo-accelerators.git cd open-healthcare-choreo-accelerators/miscellaneous/audit-service bal run The service is available at http://localhost:9093.

Post a sample audit event: curl -X POST http://localhost:9093/audits \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "typeCode": "rest", "subTypeCode": "read", "actionCode": "R", "outcomeCode": "0", "recordedTime": "2024-01-15T10:30:01Z", "agentType": "humanuser", "agentName": "dr-smith", "agentIsRequestor": true, "sourceObserverName": "", "sourceObserverType": "3", "entityType": "2", "entityRole": "1", "entityWhatReference": "Patient/123" }' On success, the service returns the generated FHIR AuditEvent resource. The event is also appended to the configured log file.

FHIR facade APIs built with the Ballerina FHIR R4 service type can publish audit events to the audit service through the built-in audit handler. When a request completes, the FHIRResponseInterceptor sends the audit event asynchronously so that audit logging does not block the client response.
documents.s: Enabling Audit on FHIR Facade APIs

documents.t: Add an auditConfig block to the ResourceAPIConfig record for each FHIR API that should emit audit events: import ballerinax/health.fhir.r4; public final r4:ResourceAPIConfig patientApiConfig = { resourceType: "Patient", profiles: [ "http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/Patient" ], defaultProfile: (), searchParameters: [ // ... search parameter configuration ], operations: [], serverConfig: (), authzConfig: (), auditConfig: { enabled: true, auditServiceUrl: "http://localhost:9093" } }; Field Type Description enabled boolean Enable or disable audit event publishing (default: false) auditServiceUrl string Base URL of the audit service Pass the API config to the FHIR listener when defining the service: import ballerinax/health.fhirr4; import ballerinax/health.fhir.r4; service / on new fhirr4:Listener(9090, patientApiConfig) { isolated resource function get fhir/r4/Patient(r4:FHIRContext fhirContext) returns r4:Bundle { // Implementation } }

The audit handler (handleAuditEvent in ballerinax/health.fhir.r4) builds an InternalAuditEvent from the request context and posts it to POST /audits on the configured audit service. The handler populates the following fields automatically: Field Source typeCode Fixed as rest subTypeCode FHIR REST interaction (for example, read, vread, create) actionCode Derived from interaction: R (read), C (create), U (update), D (delete), E (other) outcomeCode 0 on success, 8 when the request is in an error state recordedTime Current UTC time agentName Authenticated user ID, or Unknown if not available agentIsRequestor true sourceObserverType 3 (Application Server) entityType 2 (System Object) entityRole 1 (Patient) entityWhatReference Raw request path from the FHIR context The HTTP client used to call the audit service is configured with retries (3 attempts, 5-second interval, exponential backoff). If publishing still fails after retries, the error and audit payload are logged by the FHIR facade.

The audit service converts each InternalAuditEvent into a FHIR R4 AuditEvent resource. A typical event generated from a Patient read request looks like this: { "resourceType": "AuditEvent", "id": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890", "type": { "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/audit-event-type", "code": "rest", "display": "RESTful Operation" }, "subtype": [{ "system": "http://hl7.org/fhir/restful-interaction", "code": "read", "display": "read" }], "action": "R", "outcome": "0", "recorded": "2024-01-15T10:30:01Z", "agent": [{ "type": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/extra-security-role-type", "code": "humanuser" }] }, "who": {"display": "dr-smith"}, "requestor": true }], "source": { "observer": {"display": "wso2fhirserver.com"}, "type": [{ "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/security-source-type", "code": "3" }] }, "entity": [{ "type": { "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/audit-entity-type", "code": "2" }, "role": { "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/object-role", "code": "1" }, "what": {"reference": "Patient/123"} }] } Audit events are persisted as newline-delimited JSON in the configured log file. For FHIR-native storage and search, you can forward events to an AuditEvent repository or implement a custom persistence layer on top of the audit log.

While AuditEvent resources record who did what and when, Provenance resources track the origin and lineage of clinical data—who created or transmitted a resource and what activity produced it. Provenance is a separate FHIR resource type. Applications that need provenance tracking should create Provenance resources explicitly when data is created, updated, or transmitted. For example, US Core requires provenance information for transmitted data—see US Core Provenance Requirements. { "resourceType": "Provenance", "target": [{"reference": "Observation/789"}], "recorded": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z", "activity": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-DataOperation", "code": "CREATE" }] }, "agent": [ { "type": {"coding": [{"code": "author"}]}, "who": {"reference": "Practitioner/dr-smith"} }, { "type": {"coding": [{"code": "transmitter"}]}, "who": {"reference": "Organization/hospital-a"} } ] }

Audit logging supports regulatory requirements for access tracking and accountability: Regulation Relevance HIPAA Audit controls (§164.312(b)) require logging access to PHI GDPR Accountability principle requires demonstrable access records

This integration leverages WSO2 IS as the OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect authorization server and WSO2 APIM as the FHIR API gateway. In this guide, we will walk through the steps to configure the SMART on FHIR flow using the Healthcare Accelerator.
documents.s: Configuring SMART on FHIR for Standalone Launch

documents.t: WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0 with WSO2 Updates applied up to update level 12 or later. The Consent Management API v2 (/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0) is available from IS 7.3.0 update level 12 onwards, and the consent management feature of WSO2 IS is used to capture and manage patient consents. Install and setup the WSO2 API Manager for Healthcare and WSO2 Identity for Healthcare. Setup IS as Third Party Key Manager for APIM. Running FHIR server. Published FHIR APIs in WSO2 APIM.

This application will be used to get an access token to access the management APIs, including the Consent Management API of WSO2 IS, by the supporting Ballerina services. Log in to the IS Admin Console(https://localhost:9453/console). Create an application of type M2M. Go to the 'Protocols' section of the application and copy the 'Client ID' and 'Client secret' values. These values will be used in the Ballerina services to securely access the management APIs. Go to the 'API Authorization' section of the application and authorize the following API resources with the listed scopes. API resource Scopes Consent Management V2 Purposes API internal_consent_mgt_purpose_view Consent Management V2 Elements API internal_consent_mgt_element_view Consent Management V2 Consents API internal_consent_mgt_consent_create, internal_consent_mgt_consent_view, internal_consent_mgt_consent_update SCIM2 Users API internal_user_mgt_view, internal_user_mgt_list Select the tenant (/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/... and /scim2/Users) variant of each API resource, not the organization (/o/...) variant. To create the consent purpose in step 6, also authorize internal_consent_mgt_purpose_create and internal_consent_mgt_element_create. note The same management application is used to access both the consent management APIs and the other WSO2 IS management APIs. No separate application is required for consent management.

Service extensions required for the SMART on FHIR flow are available in the WSO2 Healthcare Accelerator GitHub repository. Clone the repository and navigate to the extensions/services directory. consent-app-bff is the backend service for the consent app which will be used to capture the patient consent during the SMART on FHIR flow. Click here to see more about consent-app-bff service consent-app-bff is the backend for the consent app frontend which is a React application that provides the user interface to capture patient consents during the SMART on FHIR flow. Consent app bff exposes APIs to capture and manage patient consents and also serves the consent app frontend. Configure the Config.toml file of the service extension. Key Description Example Value hostname Hostname of the service localhost port Port on which the service will run 9092 corsAllowedOrigin Allowed origin for CORS configuration to allow the consent app frontend to call the APIs exposed by this service. http://localhost:3000 idpBaseUrl Base URL of the Identity Server instance. This will be used to call the management APIs, including the consent management APIs, to manage consents. https://localhost:9453 idpTokenEndpoint Token endpoint of the Identity Server instance. This will be used to obtain access tokens to call the management APIs. https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token consentContextApiTrustStorePath Path to the truststore file containing the certificates required to establish SSL connection with the Identity Server when calling the management APIs. `` consentContextApiTrustStorePassword Truststore password. This will be used to establish SSL connection with the Identity Server when calling the management APIs. `` clientId Client ID of the management application created in the previous step. This will be used to obtain access tokens to call the management APIs. `` clientSecret Client secret of the management application created in the previous step. This will be used to obtain access tokens to call the management APIs. `` ehrContextResolveUrl EHR launch context endpoint URL. This will be used to resolve the patient ID from the EHR launch context if launch scopes present in the token request. https://ehr.example.com/launch-context consentFlow Type of the consent flow to be used. Supported values are scope and purpose. For SMART on FHIR use scope as the value scope serviceId Service identifier recorded on every consent created in WSO2 IS (the serviceId field of the consent). Also used to find the user's existing consents. smart-on-fhir consentApiBasePath Base path of the WSO2 IS Consent Management API relative to idpBaseUrl. For a tenant, use /t/<tenant-domain>/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0. /api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0 alwaysAllowedScopes List of scopes that bypass consent checks in the consent app. This will be used to allow certain scopes without requiring explicit patient consent during the SMART on FHIR flow. ["openid", "internal_user_mgt_list"] singleConsentPerUser Whether to allow only a single active consent per user. If set to true, when a new consent is created for a user, all existing active consents for that user will be revoked, including consents for other services. true showConsentElements Whether to show the consent elements in the consent app frontend. If set to true, the scopes and purposes will be shown in the consent app frontend to allow users to make informed decisions when giving consent. false scopeConsent.purposeName Name of the consent purpose in WSO2 IS under which scope consents are recorded when creating a consent. SMART Scope Authorization iam-service-extensions contains the service extensions for the Identity Server. Click here to see more about iam-service-extensions service iam-service-extension is a Ballerina service that contains the following extensions to enhance the token issuance and introspection flows in IS to support SMART on FHIR use cases. Pre-issue access token extension(/pre-issue-access-token) — Invoked before issuing an access token. Adds healthcare specific claims such as patient and consent_id to the access token based on the user and the context of the request. Pre-issue ID token extension(/pre-issue-id-token) — Invoked before issuing an ID token. Adds the fhirUser claim to the ID token based on the user and the context of the request. Introspection extension(/introspect) — Invoked during token introspection. Adds healthcare specific information to the introspection response based on the token and the context of the request. Configure the Config.toml file of the service extension. Key Description Example Value hostname Hostname of the service localhost port Port on which the service will run 9093 ehrContextResolveUrl EHR launch context endpoint URL. This will be used to resolve the patient ID from the EHR launch context if launch scopes present in the token request. https://ehr.example.com/launch-context consentApiPath Path of the WSO2 IS Consent Management API relative to isBaseUrl. /api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0 consentServiceId Must match serviceId of the consent-app-bff service. Used to find the user's consent during the token request. smart-on-fhir isBaseUrl Base URL of the IS instance. This will be used for SCIM lookup and token introspection. https://localhost:9453 scimApiPath Path to the SCIM API. Defaults to /scim2/Users if not provided. https://localhost:9453/scim2/Users scimClientId OAuth2 client ID of the management application, used to call the SCIM API and the consent management API. It must be authorized for internal_user_mgt_view and internal_consent_mgt_consent_view. `` scimClientSecret OAuth2 client secret for SCIM API authentication. `` scimTokenEndpoint Token endpoint to obtain the SCIM API access token. https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token scimPatientGroupName Name of the user group used to identify patient users in the SCIM lookup. patient fhirUserAttributeName Name of the SCIM custom attribute that holds the FHIR user reference. fhirUser patientAttributeName Name of the SCIM custom attribute that holds the patient resource reference. patient alwaysAllowedScopes List of scopes that bypass consent checks in the pre-issue access token extension. ["openid", "internal_user_mgt_list"] trustStorePath Path to the truststore file containing the certificates required to establish SSL connection with other components. `` trustStorePassword Truststore password `` Go to each service directory and build the service. bal build Create a Config.toml file and add the required configurations. You can refer to the sample Config.toml.example files available inside each of the service. Start the services using the following command. Ballerina Java bal run java -jar target/bin/<service-jar-file>.jar note You can use the client credentials of the management application created in the previous step to configure the services to access the management APIs securely.
documents.s: 2. Setup and Deploy Pre built Ballerina services

documents.t: Log in to the IS Console (https://localhost:9453/console). Navigate to the Actions section from the left menu. Setup Pre Issue Access Token and Pre Issue ID Token actions with the iam-service-extensions Ballerina service path. Pre Issue Access Token - https://<pre-issue-extension-base-path>:<PORT>/pre-issue-access-token Pre Issue ID Token - https://<pre-issue-extension-base-path>:<PORT>/pre-issue-id-token

Log in to the IS Admin Console (https://localhost:9453/console). Go to User Attributes & Stores -> Attributes and create new user attributes. patient practitioner fhirUser In the fhirUser attribute, mark Required for Administrator Console and End-User Profile under Attribute Configurations.

Go to User Management -> Groups and create new groups. patient - assigned to all patient users. practitioner - assigned to all clinical staff users. Add appropriate roles to the groups. note The exact group names used here must be configured in the Config.toml of the pre-issue-access-token-service-extension (see scimPatientGroupName key).

Consent management is a built-in feature of WSO2 Identity Server (Consent Management API v2 is available from IS 7.3.0 update level 12 onwards) and it is used to capture and manage patient consents during the SMART on FHIR flow. No separate consent management system needs to be deployed. The Ballerina services access the consent management APIs of WSO2 IS using the management application created in Step 1. Enable the Consent Management API v2 by adding the following to <WSO2_IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml and restarting the Identity Server. [consent_mgt] enable_v2_api = true note If your Identity Server database already existed before updating the product (for example, the default H2 databases), apply the consent migration script <WSO2_IS_HOME>/dbscripts/migrations/consent/<db-type>-migration.txt to the identity database. Otherwise the consent APIs return 500 errors. Create the consent purpose that wraps the SMART scopes. The consent app records every approved SMART consent against this purpose, and the service fails to start if the purpose configured in scopeConsent.purposeName does not exist. Get a token with the management application and create an element and a purpose. TOKEN=$(curl -sk -u <CLIENT_ID>:<CLIENT_SECRET> https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token \ -d 'grant_type=client_credentials&scope=internal_consent_mgt_element_create internal_consent_mgt_purpose_create' | jq -r .access_token) # For the super tenant, use the path below as is. For another tenant, use # https://localhost:9453/t/<tenant-domain>/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0 CONSENT_API=https://localhost:9453/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0 ELEMENT_ID=$(curl -sk $CONSENT_API/elements \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"name": "SMART Scopes", "displayName": "SMART on FHIR scopes", "description": "Access to patient data requested by a SMART on FHIR app"}' | jq -r .id) curl -sk $CONSENT_API/purposes \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"name\": \"SMART Scope Authorization\", \"description\": \"Authorization of SMART on FHIR scopes\", \"type\": \"SMART\", \"version\": \"v1\", \"elements\": [{\"id\": \"$ELEMENT_ID\", \"mandatory\": true}]}" The approved SMART scopes themselves are stored as a property of each consent, so a single element is enough.

documents.t: Invoke the well-known configuration to get the details about auth endpoint and token endpoint. https://localhost:8243/r4/.well-known/smart-configuration You will get a JSON response as below. { "response_types_supported": [ "code", "id_token", "token", "device", "id_token token" ], "capabilities": [ "launch-standalone", "client-public", "client-confidential-symmetric", "context-standalone-patient", "sso-openid-connect", "permission-patient", "permission-offline" ], "code_challenge_methods_supported": "S256", "grant_types_supported": [ "authorization_code", "client_credentials" ], "jwks_uri": "https://localhost:9453/oauth2/jwks", "revocation_endpoint": "https://localhost:9453/oauth2/revoke", "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [ "client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post" ], "scopes_supported": [ "openid", "launch/patient", "patient/*.cruds", "user/*.cruds" ], "issuer": "https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token", "authorization_endpoint": "https://localhost:9453/oauth2/authorize", "token_endpoint": "https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token" }

Execute the following request in the URL. https://localhost:9443/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=[CLIENT_ID]&scope=fhirUser launch/patient offline_access openid patient/DiagnosticReport.s patient/Patient.r&redirect_uri=[REDIRECT_URL]&code_challenge=[CODE_CHALLENGE]&code_challenge_method=S256 Replace the REDIRECT_URL, CLIENT_ID with the values received from Step 3. CODE_CHALLENGE is the base64 URL encoded value of the SHA256 hash of a random string (code_verifier) that you generate. You can use online tools to generate the code_challenge and code_verifier values. Once redirected to the Authentication Portal sign in with the practitioner or the patient user you created at step 2. Select the permissions and the consent period and click on 'Authorize' button. If you logged in with the practitioner user, you will be asked to select a patient for the session. Select the patient and click on 'Proceed' button. Copy the 'code' value from the URL once user is redirected to the configured redirect URL after successful authentication. Execute the following curl command. curl --location --request POST 'https://localhost:9453/oauth2/token?grant_type=authorization_code&code=[CODE_VALUE]&redirect_uri=[REDIRECT_URL]&code_verifier=[CODE_VERIFIER]' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \ --header 'Authorization: Basic <base64>(CONSUMER_KEY:CONSUMER_SECRET)' You will get the access_token along with the id_token. Decoded access token looks similar to below. { "sub": "2afba262-dc62-41d6-ad05-30a30c3d6e35", "aut": "APPLICATION_USER", "iss": "https://host.docker.internal:9453/oauth2/token", "client_id": "kp3os6qrkdK1fpFN1tuW4hgRsKwa", "aud": "kp3os6qrkdK1fpFN1tuW4hgRsKwa", "nbf": 1779172841, "azp": "kp3os6qrkdK1fpFN1tuW4hgRsKwa", "patient": "102", "org_id": "10084a8d-113f-4211-a0d5-efe36b082211", "scope": "fhirUser launch/patient offline_access openid patient/DiagnosticReport.s patient/Patient.r", "exp": 1779176441, "org_name": "Super", "iat": 1779172841, "jti": "3a5a97a0-563f-40c4-b115-596d43a675d8", "consent_id": "b11a7510-73dd-4d29-9834-5903e4cc1b47", "org_handle": "carbon.super" } note consent_id and patient claims are added to the token. The consent is shared between the authorization and token requests as follows. When the user approves the consent in the consent app, consent-app-bff creates the consent in WSO2 IS for the user and serviceId, and stores the OAuth client_id of the app and the approved scopes as consent properties. When the access token is requested, the pre-issue access token extension finds the user's active consent with the user ID and the client_id of the token request, adds its ID as the consent_id claim, and removes any requested scope that the user did not approve. When singleConsentPerUser is set to true in consent-app-bff, creating a new consent revokes all of that user's other active consents, including consents recorded for other services, so the user has only one active consent overall. Set it to false if the same user's consents for other services must stay active. The decoded id token looks similar to below. { "isk": "e55c51e29b4aa647d8f4d2cc36dd74a017c1b2a4e129152d37eb4efcbc7e5064", "at_hash": "9jAg6VhwF7O05KDtmv6o0A", "sub": "2afba262-dc62-41d6-ad05-30a30c3d6e35", "amr": [ "BasicAuthenticator" ], "iss": "https://host.docker.internal:9453/oauth2/token", "nonce": "nonce", "fhirUser": "Practitioner/232421413", "sid": "472df030-be44-49ca-9ddb-a5a54699ffbd", "c_hash": "3POJLb9ayH2pNNvFaRWfTg", "aud": "kp3os6qrkdK1fpFN1tuW4hgRsKwa", "nbf": 1779172842, "azp": "kp3os6qrkdK1fpFN1tuW4hgRsKwa", "org_id": "10084a8d-113f-4211-a0d5-efe36b082211", "org_name": "Super", "exp": 1779176442, "iat": 1779172842, "jti": "6425e15f-bfde-4360-9201-f86e51a8939b", "org_handle": "carbon.super" } note fhirUser claim is added to the id token.

documents.t: Use the access_token obtained in Step 6 to call the FHIR APIs published in WSO2 APIM. Include the access token in the Authorization header of your API request: curl --location 'https://localhost:8243/r4/Patient/[PATIENT_ID]' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer [ACCESS_TOKEN]' Example requests: # Retrieve patient demographics curl --location 'https://localhost:8243/r4/Patient/102' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer [ACCESS_TOKEN]' # Retrieve diagnostic reports for a patient curl --location 'https://localhost:8243/r4/DiagnosticReport?patient=102' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer [ACCESS_TOKEN]' note The patient claim in the access token (e.g., "patient": "102") contains the Patient ID scoped to the session. Use this value to construct patient-specific FHIR queries.
